Chapter 6: Working Directly with Specific Lifetraps
Now that you’ve started to build some self-awareness and made those first, gentle shifts in your behavior, it’s time to get a bit more hands-on with the lifetraps that show up in your life. Each one has its own emotional tone and set of hurdles, so the way you work with them needs to be just as unique—almost like tending a garden, where every plant asks for its own kind of care.
So, let’s walk through a few of the most common lifetraps and see how you can start loosening their grip.
First up is Abandonment. If this one sounds familiar, you might notice anxiety or even panic bubbling up when a relationship feels shaky. The path forward? It’s all about slowly building trust in your connections. Let’s say a friend is running late, or your partner seems a little distant—it’s easy to jump to worst-case scenarios, right? But next time, try pausing before you react. Remind yourself that someone’s absence doesn’t always mean rejection. These moments of reassurance, even tiny ones, start to rewrite the old story you’ve been telling yourself.
Then there’s Defectiveness. This lifetrap whispers that you’re unlovable or flawed—pretty tough stuff to carry around. Here’s where you gently notice those moments of self-criticism and ask yourself, “Is this really true? Where’s the evidence?” You can also look for small experiences of acceptance—maybe you share something vulnerable with a friend and just notice their response. Every positive moment, no matter how small, helps tip the scales away from that harsh inner voice.
What about Unrelenting Standards? If you’re driven by perfectionism or never feel satisfied, try experimenting with “good enough” instead of perfect. Set goals that are actually realistic, and allow yourself to make mistakes. When you feel that urge to overwork or criticize yourself, see if you can respond with a bit of self-kindness instead. Over time, you’ll notice the pressure start to lift—and real satisfaction becomes a little more reachable.
Now let’s talk about Subjugation. This is the habit of always putting others first, even when it costs you. Start by noticing those situations where you automatically say yes, or push your own needs aside. Practice expressing a small preference or sharing a need, even if it feels awkward at first. Each time you speak up, you build confidence—and gradually, your relationships start to feel more balanced.
Finally, there’s Vulnerability. Living with this lifetrap can feel like you’re waiting for disaster around every corner. The way forward is to gently face your fears, step by step. Maybe you’re anxious about driving—try starting with a short, safe trip and see how it goes. Each successful experience is proof that the world isn’t quite as dangerous as your worries might suggest.
All of these examples follow a common path. First, identify which lifetrap is getting triggered, and what tends to set it off. Notice the automatic thoughts and feelings that come up. Then, gently challenge those core beliefs—look for evidence, consider other perspectives. Try out new behaviors, starting small, and build from there. And don’t forget to seek support and celebrate your progress, no matter how small it seems.
When you work directly with each lifetrap, your journey becomes more focused and effective. Remember, the goal isn’t to erase vulnerability or become flawless. It’s about finding kinder, more flexible ways to relate to yourself—and the people around you.
